pergunta: How does the União Europeia make decisions and what are its main institutions?
emUmaFrase: The UE decides through proposals from the Comissão Europeia that are debated and approved by the Parlamento Europeu and the Councils (European and Union), while the Conselho Europeu sets the major political directions.
paraComecar:
The União Europeia (UE) is an economic and political union of 27 independent member states, created through agreements such as the Tratado de Maastricht (1993) and consolidated by the Tratado de Lisboa (2009). It operates as a set of supranational institutions – that is, bodies that exercise authority above national governments – and also through intergovernmental decisions, where the states themselves negotiate with each other.

The central institutions of the UE are seven: the Parlamento Europeu (the only body directly elected by citizens every five years), the Conselho Europeu (heads of state or government who set strategic lines), the Conselho da União Europeia (ministers of the member states who deliberate on specific areas), the Comissão Europeia (responsible for proposing laws and ensuring their implementation), the Tribunal de Justiça da União Europeia (interprets community law), the Banco Central Europeu (manages the single currency, the euro) and the Tribunal de Contas Europeia (oversees the UE’s finances). Each has a distinct role, but all work together so that the UE functions as a whole.

The typical decision‑making process starts with the Comissão Europeia, which drafts legislative proposals. These proposals are sent to the Parlamento Europeu and the Conselho da União Europeia, which examine, amend, and, as a rule, must agree for the law to be adopted – known as the ordinary legislative procedure. Meanwhile, the Conselho Europeu sets the political priorities that guide the work of the other institutions. Thus, decision‑making combines supranational initiative (Comissão) with intergovernmental approval (Conselho) and democratic control (Parlamento).

historia:
After the end of World II, Europe was devastated; Germany lay in ruins and France, although victorious, suffered severe economic losses (source [0]). On 9 May 1950, the French Foreign Minister, Robert Schuman, issued the Schuman Declaration, proposing a transnational authority to manage coal and steel production, marking the start of European integration (source [0]).

In 1951 the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) was created, followed in 1957 by the Treaty of Rome, which established the European Economic Community (EEC), expanding cooperation into a common market (source [0]).

The 1990s brought the consolidation of the union: the Maastricht Treaty, signed in 1992 and effective from 1993, established the European Union as we know it today, introducing pillars such as foreign policy and a single currency (source [0]). In 1999 the euro was launched as the single currency of the euro area, strengthening economic integration (source [0]).

In the 2000s the EU underwent institutional reforms: the Treaty of Lisbon, signed in 2007, entered into force in 2009, merging the three pillars into a single legal entity and reinforcing the role of supranational institutions (source [0]). In 2020 the United Kingdom became the only member state to leave the Union, showing that integration, though deep, remains based on sovereign decisions of the countries (source [1]).

comoFunciona:
The European Union operates through a set of seven supranational institutions that function independently but are interlinked. They are: the European Parliament (the only directly elected body), the Council of the European Union (ministers of the member states), the European Commission (executive), the European Council (heads of state or government), the European Central Bank, the Court of Justice of the European Union and the European Court of Auditors. Each institution has specific competences, but all are bound by the treaties that give the EU its own legal personality (Treaty of Maastricht, Lisbon).

In the legislative process, the European Commission has the initiative role: it drafts legislative proposals that are sent to the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. These two bodies share decision‑making power – the Parliament represents the citizens (elected every five years) and the Council represents the national governments. When both approve the text under the same conditions, the law enters into force. The European Council, although it does not legislate, sets the broad political directions that guide the actions of the Commission and other bodies.

The EU's financial side is centralized in a budget approved by the member states. The annual and multi‑annual budget is overseen by the European Court of Auditors, while the application of rules and the interpretation of the treaties are the responsibility of the Court of Justice. The monetary policy of the euro area, which brings together the countries that have adopted the euro, is conducted by the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates and ensures price stability.

Thus, EU decisions – from creating single‑market rules to defining monetary policy – result from a balance between the supranational initiative of the Commission, the democratic representation of the Parliament, and the sovereignty of the member states in the Council. This arrangement allows the EU to regulate the free movement of people, goods, services and capital, and to fund common projects, while each country retains autonomy in areas not transferred to the community sphere.

vertentes.pensa: The European Union decides through supranational and intergovernmental institutions, such as the Commission, Parliament and Council.
vertentes.quemDefende: EU institutions, scholars and official EU documents
vertentes.porQue: These institutions were created by the treaties (Maastricht, Lisbon) to ensure joint decisions in areas agreed upon by the Member States.
vertentes.criticas: The complexity of the system can generate slowness and a lack of transparency for citizens.

vertentes.pensa: The EU should cut overall spending and seek new revenues, such as a digital tax on large technology companies.
vertentes.quemDefende: President of the European Council António Costa, European Commission, some European governments
vertentes.porQue: Cutting €204‑100 billion from the budget allows balancing the accounts and financing priorities such as defence and the green transition, while the digital tax provides stable resources.
vertentes.criticas: The cuts could harm social programmes and the proposal to tax Big Tech faces resistance from countries that have large digital firms.

vertentes.pensa: The EU should maintain a large pool of resources (around €100 billion) to support Ukraine in the war against Russia.
vertentes.quemDefende: Ukraine, EU authorities dealing with foreign policy, Ukrainian media
vertentes.porQue: Without this financial support, Ukraine would lose defence and reconstruction capacity, compromising European security.
vertentes.criticas: Allocating so much money to Ukraine could limit resources for other internal EU priorities.

vertentes.pensa: The United Kingdom seeks to re‑establish a close relationship with the EU, negotiating trade and mobility agreements after Brexit.
vertentes.quemDefende: British government (Prime Minister Andy Burnham), EU representatives in bilateral negotiations
vertentes.porQue: A “reset” allows the United Kingdom to access European markets and cooperate in strategic areas such as food, carbon and youth mobility.
vertentes.criticas: The EU may see the proposal as an attempt to circumvent Brexit rules and demand concessions that compromise internal integration.

vertentes.pensa: The EU ignores Russian interests by equating Europe with the European Union and NATO, preventing any security dialogue.
vertentes.quemDefende: Russian senator Konstantin Kosachev, Russian state media (TASS)
vertentes.porQue: While the EU expands its security policy, it excludes Russia, which, they say, eliminates the basis for commitments.
vertentes.criticas: The criticism overlooks the fact that the EU is a union of sovereign Member States that set their own security policy.

vertentes.pensa: The EU proposal to tax large digital companies is seen as a legitimate way to fund the European budget.
vertentes.quemDefende: The Hindu newspaper, centre‑left Indian analysts
vertentes.porQue: A digital tax creates a progressive revenue source that can be used for common projects, without overburdening national taxpayers.
vertentes.criticas: The measure could generate trade disputes with countries that view unilateral taxation as such and affect foreign investments.

ondeConcordam: All sides recognize that the EU has a set of institutions (Commission, Parliament, Council) that take part in decisions and that the EU budget is a subject of political debate.
ondeBrigam: The main point of disagreement lies in budgetary priorities (cuts vs maintaining funds for Ukraine), the introduction of new digital taxes, and the nature of the EU's relationship with external actors such as the United Kingdom and Russia.
eHoje: France 24 (21/11/2026) reported that the EU and the United Kingdom signed three agreements to simplify food exports, align emissions trading schemes, and facilitate youth mobility, showing how EU decisions affect recent trade relations.

cadeia.passo: The European Commission drafts legislative proposals that affect the EU internal market.
The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union examine, amend and adopt these proposals.
The adopted laws set commercial and regulatory standards for products circulating in the EU.
These standards determine access requirements for Brazilian exporters, such as sanitary standards or tariffs.
Consequently, Brazilian exporters adjust their processes, which can change prices and export volumes to the European market.
